analysis.one_liner: Caps rent increases and evictions by large landlords, funds lawyers for tenants, and bans housing discrimination by income source.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of its three committees and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place a federal ceiling on rent increases by landlords who own more than five properties, let them evict tenants only for listed reasons (like missing rent for two straight months), and require them to keep units in good repair. It would ban landlords from rejecting tenants because they pay with housing vouchers, Social Security, or child support; give tenants federal grants for a right to a lawyer in eviction court; spend heavily on removing lead and other hazards from homes; and cut off federal mortgage backing and insurance from the largest, worst-acting landlords. It also rewards state and local governments that allow more affordable housing with a bigger federal share of highway costs, and penalizes those that restrict it.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in buildings owned by large landlords, who would gain a cap on rent increases, protection from no-cause evictions, and a right to sue. Renters with housing vouchers or non-wage income would gain legal protection from source-of-income discrimination. Low-income tenants facing eviction could get a government-paid lawyer. Families in older homes would benefit from lead and hazard removal funding. Legal immigrants excluded from federal housing aid since 1996 would become eligible again.

how_it_helps.text: Landlords owning more than five residential properties could not raise rent above the greater of the local Consumer Price Index increase or 3 percent of the unit's average monthly rent, could evict only for specified reasons such as missing rent for two or more consecutive months, and had to keep units in good repair.

Tenants could sue violating landlords in federal court, leases could not waive that right, and state attorneys general could seek damages of up to ten times monthly rent on behalf of affected residents.

The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to ban discrimination based on 'source of income,' explicitly covering housing vouchers, Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, child support, and other lawful income — stopping landlords who refuse voucher holders.
HUD could grant $6.5 billion a year to states and localities to guarantee tenants a lawyer in eviction proceedings, with at least 85 percent of funds spent directly on legal representation.
The bill would authorize $10 billion a year for removing lead paint and other housing hazards, mostly through the existing Lead Hazard Reduction Program.

Large rental owners (more than 100 units in one metro area, 1,000 nationwide, or units in three states) could no longer buy federally backed mortgages or mortgage-backed securities, obtain federal mortgage insurance, or buy foreclosed FHA properties — and at least 75 percent of FHA foreclosed homes would have to go to owner-occupants, nonprofits, community land trusts, or community-controlled entities.
The bill would restore eligibility for federal housing assistance to nonresident aliens, repealing 1996 welfare-law restrictions and the 1980 housing provision that bars them.

States and localities that encourage affordable housing — by speeding permits, allowing denser development, banning source-of-income discrimination, or taxing vacant land — would get a bigger federal share of highway project costs; jurisdictions with exclusionary rules like large minimum lot sizes or parking mandates would get a smaller share.

analysis.who_pays: Large landlords and corporate rental owners, who would face rent caps, eviction limits, repair mandates, public disclosure of evictions and fees, and loss of access to federally backed mortgage financing. Federal taxpayers would fund the grant programs, roughly $16.5 billion a year in authorizations. Some small landlords with four or fewer properties would escape all the new rules, creating an incentive to stay under the threshold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large landlords and corporate rental owners

drawbacks.text: The rent cap applies only to landlords with more than five properties, so an owner could avoid it by splitting holdings — and the cap itself is generous, set at the greater of CPI inflation or 3 percent, which in high-cost markets can still mean large annual increases.

Rent caps and just-cause eviction rules can discourage investment in rental housing and reduce supply over time, a trade-off even supporters of tenant protections generally acknowledge; a poorly designed cap can push landlords toward conversions or neglect.

The bill would cut off federal mortgage backing and insurance for any entity owning more than 1,000 units nationwide or units in three states — by size alone, before any finding of wrongdoing — which could freeze financing for some large, lawful operators and complicate multifamily lending markets.

Tying the federal share of highway funding to local zoning and landlord rules would tie routine transportation money to housing policy, and jurisdictions that lose federal match could shift costs to their own taxpayers.
The $6.5 billion and $10 billion annual authorizations are large new federal spending commitments lasting a decade each.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tenant protections are real but aimed squarely at corporate landlords, leaving most small landlords untouched — a deliberate design choice that limits the burden while also creating a threshold loophole. The rent cap is modest (inflation or 3 percent), so the strongest economic objection applies with less force than to strict rent control. The largest costs are fiscal: roughly $16.5 billion a year in authorizations, plus the risk that barring the biggest landlords from federal financing disrupts multifamily lending. On balance the bill would shift bargaining power from large landlords to tenants, which is precisely why landlord interests would fight it; the serious design questions are about the financing cutoffs and the highway-money lever, not the core tenant protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, passed along to two subcommittees, and never came up for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on November 13, 2019, as part of her 'A Just Society' legislative package, with four Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Financial Services, Judiciary, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, and later to subcommittees in November and December 2019.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the action record, and the House never voted on it; it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large landlords and corporate rental owners, who avoided rent caps, just-cause eviction rules, public disclosure requirements, and the loss of access to federally backed financing. Nothing changed for the renters the bill was written to protect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large landlords and corporate rental owners

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as part of her A Just Society package and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Reps. Grace Meng, Rashida Tlaib, Chuy García, and Barbara Lee
4 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other member of the House signed on.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the committee with jurisdiction over its core rent-cap and landlord provisions; the record shows no action after referral.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; the referral to the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee in December 2019 was the last action on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration by his committee, which held jurisdiction over its highway funding provisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five sponsors were all House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it; because it never reached a vote, there is no roll-call record of how the full chambers would have split.

industries.industry: Large landlords and corporate rental owners
industries.note: The bill would cap their rent increases, restrict evictions to listed causes, require repairs and public disclosure of evictions and fees, and cut off federally backed mortgage financing for the largest operators. Their business model — raising rents, charging fees, and evicting at scale — is exactly what the provisions target.

industries.industry: Multifamily lenders and mortgage-backed securities markets
industries.note: Lending to and securitizing loans for large rental owners would become legally impossible under the bill, removing a large class of borrowers from federally supported markets. Smaller landlords and owner-occupied lending would be unaffected.
A $6.5 billion annual grant program would fund lawyers for tenants in eviction proceedings, a major new revenue stream for legal aid and tenant attorneys.
$10 billion a year for HUD's lead hazard and healthy homes programs would fund testing and removal work in older housing stock.
